lines: You took the 1,000 dollar bonus now. A week later, 600 of it went on a phone, because the sale ended tonight and it felt like free money. Meanwhile you owe 600 dollars on a card at 24 percent. Paying it off would have saved 144 dollars a year.
Mental accounting is sorting money into jars by where it came from. But a dollar is a dollar, whether it's a bonus or your paycheck.
Loss aversion: a loss feels about twice as strong as a gain of the same size. A coin flip that wins 150 or loses 100 pays 25 dollars on average, yet most people say no.
Present bias is wanting things now, even when waiting pays. Anchoring is when the first number you see, like a was-200-dollars tag, shapes how every price after it feels.

Herd behavior is following the crowd, usually after the price has already jumped. Overconfidence is thinking you can predict better than you can. The households that traded the most earned 11.4 percent a year, while the market made 17.9.
The fix is to make good choices automatic. When one company signed workers up for its retirement plan automatically, participation jumped from 37 to 86 percent.
So before a big money choice: pause, name the trap, do the math, and set a rule.
